projects.name: Librora
projects.oneLiner: Reading companion: track reading, manage book collection, discover insights.
projects.essence: User-facing reading tracker / personal library product. Helps users build reading habits, organize their book collections, track progress, and discover new books based on their preferences.

hosting.name: Vercel
hosting.notes: Root directory set to apps/web; Vercel builds the web app only

instructions.localSetupMd:
## Local Setup

```bash
npm install
npm run dev          # web on :7777
npm run dev:mobile   # Expo
```

Firebase config files are committed: the OAuth client ids are public and security comes from domain restrictions.
instructions.deployMd:
## Deployment

**Web** — Vercel, root directory `apps/web`.

**Mobile** —
```bash
eas build --platform ios --profile production
eas submit --platform ios
```

Native modules such as react-native-view-shot need a dev client rebuild before they work.
instructions.knownIssuesMd:
## Known Issues

- Nested modals do not work on iOS; switch views inside one modal instead.
- Lending goes through /api/loans rather than Firestore directly, because the security rules for `loans` are incomplete.

security.authMethod: Firebase Auth — Google and Apple sign-in, email/password on web
security.dataEncryption: In transit by the provider; Firestore encrypts at rest
security.complianceNotes: Apple requires Sign in with Apple wherever a social login is offered.

components.name: Web app
components.notes: Stripe for subscriptions — web only, never iOS.

components.name: iOS app
components.oneLiner: Barcode scanning, reading timer, offline library.
components.notes: Apple IAP for Pro; Sign in with Apple is required by App Store review.

components.name: Home screen widgets
components.oneLiner: Small, medium and large widgets showing reading stats.
components.notes: Reads stats through App Group group.io.librora.app.

components.name: Reading timer Live Activity
components.oneLiner: Dynamic Island and lock screen timer.
components.notes: iOS 16.2+. Bridged from JS via LiveActivityModule.swift.

components.name: Shared core
components.oneLiner: Types, Zod schemas, subscription limits, ISBN utilities.
components.notes: Imported by both web and mobile as @librora/core.

decisions.title: Database
decisions.rationale: The mobile app has to work with no signal — on a train, in a library basement. Firestore gives offline persistence and conflict resolution without writing a sync layer, which for a two-platform product built by one person is the whole argument.
decisions.alternatives: Postgres with a hand-written sync layer. Cheaper per read and far better at the reporting the Insights page wants, but offline sync is months of work and the hardest kind to get right.
decisions.tradeoffs: Queries are weak: anything resembling a join or an aggregate is assembled client-side. Reads are billed, so a careless listener is a bill. Pagination for getMyBooks is still deferred because the Firestore half is easy and the virtualised list is not.

decisions.title: Shared logic
decisions.rationale: Subscription limits, ISBN validation and category lists have to agree exactly between web and mobile, and the cost of them disagreeing is a user charged wrongly or a book filed twice. No React and no Firebase in it, so both platforms can import it and it can be tested on its own.
decisions.alternatives: Duplicating the rules in each app, which is what happens by default and drifts within weeks.
decisions.tradeoffs: A monorepo and its hoisting problems: the root must pin react and react-dom to 18 or the Next build breaks, because mobile is on 19.

decisions.title: Payments
decisions.choice: Stripe on web, Apple IAP on iOS
decisions.rationale: Not a preference — Apple requires in-app purchase for digital features and rejects anything that routes around it. Stripe stays on web where the fee is lower and the flow is ours.
decisions.alternatives: None available. Stripe-only would fail review.
decisions.tradeoffs: Two payment systems, two sets of webhooks, two definitions of entitlement that have to resolve to the same answer.

decisions.title: Widgets and Live Activities in Swift
decisions.rationale: WidgetKit and ActivityKit have no React Native equivalent. The timer on the lock screen and the Dynamic Island are platform features, and reaching them means native code — there is no decision to make beyond accepting it.
decisions.alternatives: Third-party bridges, which lag each iOS release.
decisions.tradeoffs: A second language in the repository, an App Group to pass data across, and native modules needing a dev client rebuild before anyone can test them.

risks.title: Firestore rules for loans are incomplete
risks.detail: Mobile lending writes through /api/loans instead of Firestore directly, specifically because the security rules for the loans collection do not cover it. The API is a workaround for a gap that is still open underneath.
risks.mitigation: Write the rules, then move the mobile client back onto Firestore directly and delete the endpoint.

risks.title: Unauthenticated public endpoints have no rate limit
risks.detail: /api/isbn-lookup and /api/google-books are public and unauthenticated. The Google Books key allows 1,000 requests a day and is shared by everyone.
risks.mitigation: Upstash Redis for shared state across Vercel instances. It must not block iOS, which calls these legitimately.

risks.title: OCR runs on a public demo key
risks.detail: OCR_SPACE_API_KEY is not set, so photo scan falls back to the key printed in OCR.space documentation and shared with everyone who copied it. Its quota is spent by strangers and can run out at any moment.
risks.mitigation: Register at ocr.space — free, email only — and set the key in Vercel and .env.local.

risks.title: Old Chronos collections never deleted
risks.detail: The migration on 2026-08-20 left users/{uid}/philosophers and users/{uid}/chronos_authors in place as a backup. They have been read by nothing since.
risks.mitigation: Delete per user in the Firebase console once the unified authors have been confirmed correct in production.

risks.title: Next.js 14 while 15 is out
risks.detail: No known blockers, but a major upgrade needs a dedicated testing pass and nothing is broken today.
risks.mitigation: Schedule it as its own piece of work rather than attaching it to a feature.

costs.notes: Required to ship on the App Store at all.
Price not recorded — check the Name.com invoice.
Hobby is free; Pro is 20/month. Which one is in use is not recorded here.
Firestore reads and storage. Spark is free with quotas; Blaze is pay-as-you-go.
25,000 a month, capped at 500 a day per IP — shared by the whole user base because calls leave from the server.

instructions.localSetupMd:
## Local Setup

```bash
npm install
npx prisma generate
npm run dev
```

The dev server caches the Prisma client in memory: after `prisma generate` it must be restarted, and a second server on port 3000 will serve a stale one.
instructions.deployMd:
## Deployment

Vercel, on push to `main`. The build runs `prisma migrate deploy` before `next build`, so a successful deployment implies the migration applied.

Commits must be authored as the Vercel account owner or the deployment sits in BLOCKED with no explanation in the CLI output.
instructions.testingMd:
## Testing

```bash
npx vitest run
```

250+ tests. The field matcher for the extension is tested against the markup real ATS systems emit, including the negative cases — filling a referrer field with your own name is worse than filling nothing.
instructions.knownIssuesMd:
## Known Issues

- `prisma migrate dev` wants a database reset because `rate_limits` is created lazily at runtime by design. Migrations are written by hand and applied with `$executeRawUnsafe`, then marked with `prisma migrate resolve --applied`.
- Sign-up is not restricted: anyone with the URL can create an account.

security.authMethod: Better Auth, Google OAuth only; email/password disabled
security.dataEncryption: OAuth tokens encrypted with the auth secret before they reach Postgres
security.complianceNotes: Holds a full job search including contacts and documents. The extension token is hashed; it is shown once and cannot be read back.

decisions.title: Database
decisions.rationale: The product is relational to its core — applications, stages, interviews, contacts, documents — and the analytics are the point. A funnel that must say "rejected at assignment" without claiming a conversion needs joins and real constraints.
decisions.alternatives: Firestore, as used in Librora. Rejected because every report would be assembled in memory and the stage model could not be enforced.
decisions.tradeoffs: No offline story, which is fine for a web app. Migrations are written by hand here because `migrate dev` wants a reset.

decisions.title: Status model
decisions.choice: Four separate fields: stage, milestones, history, outcome
decisions.rationale: A search goes interview, then assignment, then interview again. One status field cannot express "back at interviewing, having already done the assignment", and collapsing offer into hired would make the funnel claim conversions that never happened.
decisions.alternatives: A single status enum, which is what every tracker starts with and why none of them can answer that question.
decisions.tradeoffs: More to keep consistent, and a UI that had to be redesigned to show one control over two fields.

decisions.title: Generated documents are verified, not trusted
decisions.rationale: A tailored resume is read for fit, not fact-checked line by line, so an invented employer or a stretched date survives all the way to an interview. The prompt asks for good behaviour; the verifier enforces it and refuses to save a document that invents.
decisions.alternatives: Trusting the model, which fails silently and exactly where it is most expensive.
decisions.tradeoffs: A whole verification layer, and occasional refusals on documents that were fine.

decisions.title: No mailbox connection
decisions.rationale: Reading a mailbox needs restricted Gmail scopes and a CASA assessment, for a feature that pasting solves in one keystroke. The clipboard HTML even keeps the links, which is what the parser actually needs.
decisions.tradeoffs: Nothing happens automatically; the person has to paste.

decisions.title: Extension reaches pages through activeTab
decisions.rationale: Employers host the application form on their own domain, so a host list cannot cover them. activeTab grants one tab for one press and expires by itself, which gets the capability without standing permission to read every page.
decisions.alternatives: <all_urls>, which would work everywhere and ask for far more than it needs.
decisions.tradeoffs: A press is required on sites outside the list.

risks.title: Sign-up is open to anyone with the URL
risks.detail: There is no allowlist on sign-in — only on the admin area. Any Google account can create a tracker, and that data lands in the same Neon database under a privacy policy that describes a tool for one person.
risks.mitigation: An allowlist on sign-in, in the shape already used for admin. Needed before the extension link is shared.

risks.title: One Anthropic key shared with Chronos
risks.detail: The same ANTHROPIC_API_KEY serves this project and Chronos. Rotating or revoking it breaks both, and the rate limits are shared, so a busy sweep here degrades Chronos.
risks.mitigation: Separate keys per project. Deliberate for now.

risks.title: Preview deployments lack the AI key
risks.detail: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set for Production and Development but not Preview, so every AI path fails on a preview deployment with an inline message rather than an obvious error.
risks.mitigation: Set it through the Vercel REST API — the CLI cannot add Preview variables on this account.

risks.title: Holds an entire job search
risks.detail: Applications, correspondence, contacts, uploaded documents and a full CV. A breach would expose a job search to a current employer.
risks.mitigation: Extension tokens are hashed and shown once; OAuth tokens are encrypted before storage. The open sign-up above is the weak point.

costs.notes: Paid 2026-11-23. One-off, covers the account rather than the item.
Free tier is likely; not verified.
Shared with Chronos, so the spend cannot be attributed to one project.

projects.name: Femotion
projects.oneLiner: Feel. Track. Understand. — privacy-first mood, cycle and context analytics.
projects.essence: A privacy-first tracker for mood, menstrual cycle, thoughts, music and context, for iOS and web. Built around keeping the data on the device wherever possible.

components.name: iOS app
components.oneLiner: The same client wrapped with Capacitor.
components.notes: Local data through @capacitor-community/sqlite rather than the cloud.

instructions.localSetupMd:
## Local Setup

Node 24 is pinned for this project through fnm and `.nvmrc`; the global Node is untouched.

```bash
fnm exec --using=24 pnpm install
```
instructions.deployMd:
## Deployment

Firebase Hosting for the client, Firebase Functions for the backend.

The iOS build goes through Capacitor and Xcode.

operations.secretsLocation: Firebase project config; see notenv-style local files

security.dataEncryption: On-device SQLite for the sensitive records; Firestore encrypts at rest
security.complianceNotes: Holds menstrual cycle and mood data — among the most sensitive categories there are. Privacy-first is the product claim, so anything that moves data off the device needs a deliberate decision.

decisions.title: Framework
decisions.rationale: The only project here not on React, and deliberately: it is the stack worked in daily, so the product moves fastest and the habits are already right.
decisions.alternatives: React, used by everything else in this portfolio.
decisions.tradeoffs: Nothing is shared with the other projects — no common components, no common utilities.

decisions.title: iOS through Capacitor rather than React Native
decisions.rationale: The client is already an Angular web app. Capacitor ships that same app as a native shell, so one codebase covers both without rewriting the UI.
decisions.alternatives: A separate React Native app, which would mean maintaining the product twice.
decisions.tradeoffs: Native feel is limited by what the web view gives. Platform features need plugins.

decisions.title: Sensitive data stored on the device
decisions.rationale: Mood and menstrual cycle records are among the most sensitive categories there are. Privacy-first is the product claim, and the strongest form of it is data that never leaves the phone.
decisions.alternatives: Firestore for everything, which is simpler and makes the claim untrue.
decisions.tradeoffs: No sync between devices, no server-side analysis, and a backup story that has to be built rather than inherited.

risks.title: Holds reproductive health data
risks.detail: Menstrual cycle data is special-category under GDPR and legally exposed in several jurisdictions. Any feature that moves it off the device changes the legal position of the whole product.
risks.mitigation: Keep the on-device boundary explicit in code and in the privacy policy, and treat moving any of it to the cloud as a decision requiring its own review.

risks.title: On-device data has no backup path
risks.detail: SQLite on the phone means a lost or wiped phone is a total loss of history — the exact data users would be most upset to lose.
risks.mitigation: An encrypted export the user controls, so recovery does not require a server that can read it.

risks.title: Not yet submitted to the App Store
risks.detail: The iOS shell exists but has not been through review, which is where health-category apps meet the longest questionnaires.
risks.mitigation: Budget time for the health-data disclosures rather than treating submission as a formality.

costs.notes: Shared with Librora — one membership covers both.
Hosting and functions. Most data stays on the device.

projects.name: Chronos
projects.oneLiner: Authors, works and reading timelines — a companion to Librora.
projects.essence: A knowledge graph of authors and their works with a timeline, an encyclopedia and a photo gallery. Lives inside the Librora monorepo but deploys separately and has its own mobile client.

hosting.name: Vercel
hosting.notes: Separate Vercel project from the Librora web app

components.name: Web app
components.notes: Runs on port 7778 locally. Geography uses Nominatim and OSM tiles — no keyed providers.

instructions.localSetupMd:
## Local Setup

Part of the Librora monorepo.

```bash
npm install
npm run dev --workspace @librora/chronos   # :7778
```
instructions.deployMd:
## Deployment

Its own Vercel project, root directory `apps/chronos`.

security.complianceNotes: Holds reading history rather than identifying data.

decisions.title: Lives in the Librora monorepo but deploys separately
decisions.rationale: It shares types and Firebase configuration with Librora, so a separate repository would mean copying both. A separate Vercel project keeps the deployments independent, so a Chronos build cannot break librora.io.
decisions.alternatives: Its own repository, or a route inside the Librora web app.
decisions.tradeoffs: The monorepo root has to satisfy both, which is where the React 18/19 pinning comes from.

decisions.title: Maps without a keyed provider
decisions.rationale: The geography view needed to exist before anyone knew whether it would be used. Nominatim and OSM need no key, no billing account and no quota negotiation, so the feature could ship and be judged.
decisions.alternatives: Google Maps or Mapbox — better data, but a key, a card and a per-view price for a feature that might be removed.
decisions.tradeoffs: Nominatim asks for polite use and is not built for volume. Real traffic means moving to a keyed provider.

risks.title: Old collections still in Firestore
risks.detail: philosophers and chronos_authors were left after the 2026-08-20 migration as a backup and nothing reads them.
risks.mitigation: Delete per user once production is confirmed correct.

risks.title: Deprecated photoUrl still read by the UI
risks.detail: The Author type keeps photoUrl for backward compatibility and three components still read it instead of photos[0].
risks.mitigation: Move them to photos[0] after the old collections are gone.

risks.title: Nominatim has no quota guarantee
risks.detail: A free public service with a usage policy rather than a contract. It can rate-limit or block at any time.
risks.mitigation: Acceptable while usage is one person. A keyed provider before that changes.

costs.notes: A subdomain of librora.io — no separate cost, and it lapses when that domain does.
A second project on the same account.

registrations.name: chronos.librora.io
registrations.notes: Subdomain of librora.io. It has no registration of its own and dies with the parent.
